title: Scaling GitHub for your Agents — Sam Morrow, GitHub
talk_summary: Sam Morrow describes how GitHub's MCP server was scaled to ~8M tool calls/week by aggressively cutting context (tool count and output tokens), encoding agent intent server-side to reduce round trips and failures, and running evals on tool descriptions against each other. He also covers stateless per-request server construction, scope-filtered tool surfaces, and security tradeoffs around tokens and prompt injection.

takeaways.technique: Prune and group the tool surface by usage
takeaways.what_they_do: Cut the default tool set to the general case based on real usage data, grouped CRUD tools, and kept the default small (~40 tools) with opt-in expansion.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we cut the amount of context used by focusing the tools more specifically to the general case... about 49% reduction of the initial load
takeaways.numbers: ~49% reduction in initial context load; default ~40 tools; previously 100+ tools

takeaways.what_they_do: Redesigned what list/read tools return (e.g. list pull requests) to only include fields agents need, rather than dumping full API objects.
takeaways.evidence_quote: just by tailoring exactly what comes with the list pull requests, it's like actually lost more than 75% of the tokens used in the output

takeaways.technique: Encode agent intent server-side to cut round trips
takeaways.what_they_do: Instead of forcing the agent to make several calls, the server internally makes multiple API calls to fulfill one intent, reducing failures and context churn.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you might have to make five API calls to make it more robust... we do that in the server side to reduce round trips

takeaways.technique: Cross-test tool descriptions against each other
takeaways.what_they_do: Rather than micro-optimizing one tool description, they eval descriptions in a pool so each tool is called at the right times and not the wrong times.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you try to test them against each other to try and make sure that they're called at the right times and not called at the wrong times

takeaways.technique: Scope-filtered tool surface from the credential
takeaways.what_they_do: When a token is presented, the server filters the available tools down to the token's scopes; OAuth uses step-up scope challenges instead of hard failure.
takeaways.evidence_quote: if you log into GitHub MCP with a PAT token that we just immediately filter the tools down by the scopes that the token has

takeaways.what_they_do: They build a fresh server instance per request and add only the tools the caller is configured/allowed to use, with Redis for session storage and no session affinity.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we actually make a brand new in the SDK sense a brand new server instance on every single request and we add the tools to it at the start
